questions.question: In the smart‑watch trade‑off scenario, which processor choice best illustrates the “compromise” role of an ASIP between a general‑purpose MPU and a single‑purpose MCU?

options.A: Selecting a high‑performance MPU to maximize screen refresh speed.
options.B: Selecting a low‑power MCU to extend battery life at the cost of slower refresh.
options.C: Selecting an ASIP that provides moderate performance with only a modest increase in power consumption.
options.D: Selecting a dedicated SSP that can only perform a single function such as AES encryption.

questions.explanation:
The context describes ASIPs as “optimized for a particular application or domain” and positioned between MPUs (high performance, high power) and MCUs (low power, limited performance) [Page 40]. This middle‑ground matches the compromise concept in the smart‑watch trade‑off discussion [Page 35].

---

questions.question: How does an ASIP serve as a compromise between the flexibility of a general‑purpose MPU and the efficiency of a single‑purpose SSP?

options.A: By providing a fully programmable instruction set with no domain‑specific extensions.
options.B: By integrating CPU, memory, and I/O on one chip like an MCU.
options.C: By incorporating domain‑specific instructions that accelerate certain tasks while retaining programmability for other functions.
options.D: By limiting execution to only one fixed algorithm to minimize silicon area.

questions.explanation:
ASIPs combine “domain‑specific” optimization (e.g., network processors) with a programmable core, thus lying between MPUs (fully programmable) and SSPs (single‑purpose) [Page 40].

---

questions.question: Which of the following features most clearly distinguishes an ASIP from a typical MCU, based on the provided material?

options.C: Integration of CPU, memory, and I/O on a single die.
options.D: Use of a low‑power idle mode.

questions.explanation:
The table contrasts MPUs (CPU only) and MCUs (CPU + memory + I/O) [Page 43]. The ASIP is highlighted for its domain‑specific nature, implying specialized instructions not found in generic MCUs [Page 40].

options.D: SSP/SPP processor specifically designed for AES encryption

questions.explanation:
The context places “AES encryption engine” under SSP/SPP processors, indicating they are the dedicated solution for such single‑purpose tasks [Page 40].

questions.question: If a designer needs moderate flexibility to handle both network packet processing and occasional control‑loop tasks, which processor choice best aligns with the compromise nature of an ASIP?

options.A: MPU, because it can run any software without restriction.
options.B: MCU, because it offers low power but limited processing capability.
options.C: ASIP, because it provides domain‑specific acceleration for networking while remaining programmable for other tasks.
options.D: SSP, because it is optimized for a single function only.

questions.explanation:
ASIPs are described as “optimized for a particular application or domain” such as network processors, yet retain programmability, making them a compromise between MPUs and SSPs [Page 40].

---

questions.question: When replacing a general‑purpose MPU with an ASIP for a baseband signal‑processing application, which design metric is most likely to improve without a proportional increase in power consumption?

options.C: Processing efficiency for the target domain

questions.explanation:
The ASIP’s domain‑specific optimizations (e.g., baseband processing) increase efficiency for that task, while the compromise nature avoids the high power draw typical of a full MPU [Page 40].

questions.question: Which statement best explains why an ASIP can be preferable to a pure DSP for a network‑processor design, according to the context?

options.A: ASIPs always consume less power than any DSP.
options.B: ASIPs combine the programmable nature of MPUs with domain‑specific acceleration, whereas DSPs focus solely on signal‑processing workloads.
options.C: DSPs integrate CPU, memory, and I/O on a single chip, which ASIPs do not.
options.D: ASIPs are listed under “Microcontroller” in the context.

questions.explanation:
The context groups DSPs and ASIPs separately, noting that ASIPs are “network processors” while DSPs are “optimized for a particular application or domain” such as signal processing [Page 40]. This indicates ASIPs add programmable flexibility beyond pure DSP capabilities.

questions.question: In the trade‑off activity (Option A vs. Option B), which choice most closely mirrors the compromise strategy embodied by an ASIP?

options.A: Adding a low‑power mode to a MCU, sacrificing performance.
options.B: Adding a faster MPU, increasing cost and power.
options.C: Selecting an ASIP that provides a balanced increase in performance with only a modest power penalty.
options.D: Reducing battery size to shrink the device, regardless of performance.

questions.explanation:
Option C reflects the ASIP’s role as a middle ground—enhancing performance without the full power/cost penalties of a high‑end MPU, aligning with the compromise idea discussed on pages 35 and 40.

questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes the “compromise” nature of ASIPs when viewed against the definitions of MPU and MCU provided?

options.A: ASIPs eliminate the need for external memory, like MCUs.
options.B: ASIPs offer a full CPU core without any domain‑specific extensions.
options.C: ASIPs provide a CPU core with selective domain‑specific extensions, delivering better performance than MCUs while using less power than MPUs.
options.D: ASIPs are identical to MPUs but with a different branding.

questions.explanation:
The MPU definition (“CPU only; needs external memory”) [Page 43] and MCU definition (“CPU + memory + I/O on one chip”) [Page 43] contrast with ASIPs, which add domain‑specific instructions to achieve a performance‑power compromise [Page 40].
